After checking the measurement literature carefully, I would simplify the estimator slightly and **freeze the following parameter set**. The important change from our earlier discussion is that I would not try to infer hidden infrastructure parameters separately. We can construct an operational water estimate entirely from the visible transcript, the user-selected model and thinking level, and a small number of literature-calibrated coefficients.

The resulting quantity should always be called **estimated operational water consumption**, because training, chip manufacturing and other embodied effects are outside the boundary of this tool.

## 1. Final equation

For assistant response \(i\),

\[
E_i^{\rm text} =
e_m^{\rm in}(L_i)\,N_i^{\rm in}
+
e_m^{\rm out}
\left[
N_i^{\rm out}
+
r_\ell N_i^{\rm out}
\right],
\]

where \(L_i=N_i^{\rm in}\) is the visible context length, while the visible non-text operations contribute

\[
E_i^{\rm tools} =
0.04n_i^{\rm web}
+0.01n_i^{\rm code}
+0.06n_i^{\rm img,in}
+2.9n_i^{\rm img,out}
+25n_i^{\rm video}.
\]

The total electricity estimate is

\[
E_{\rm chat}=\sum_i(E_i^{\rm text}+E_i^{\rm tools}),
\]

and finally

\[
\boxed{
W_{\rm chat}=4.1\,E_{\rm chat}
}
\]

where \(E_{\rm chat}\) is in Wh and \(W_{\rm chat}\) is in mL.

I would additionally return direct and indirect water separately:

\[
W_{\rm direct}=0.2E_{\rm chat},
\]

\[
W_{\rm electricity}=3.9E_{\rm chat}.
\]

These are the central estimates. The application should also calculate a broad uncertainty interval.

---

# 2. Text-generation energy

This is the most important parameter.

The strongest recent reference is Oviedo et al. in *Joule* (2026). For an optimized production-like deployment, they estimate a median **0.31 Wh** for a standard frontier-model query with 500 input and 300 output tokens; importantly, their methodology finds output generation to dominate energy consumption and treats effective token length approximately as output length for ordinary queries. citeturn279616search0turn458839search12

Their comparison with direct measurements is particularly useful:

| Model / estimate | Output tokens | Energy |
|---|---:|---:|
| Llama 3.1 70B, ML.ENERGY | 361 | 0.04 Wh |
| Llama 3.1 70B, Caravaca et al. | 300 | 0.05 Wh |
| Llama 3.1 405B, ML.ENERGY | 367 | 0.21 Wh |
| Llama 3.1 405B, Caravaca et al. | 300 | 0.21 Wh |
| GPT-4o, Epoch estimate | 500 | 0.30 Wh |
| GPT-4o, Jegham estimate | 300 | 0.42 Wh |
| Frontier \(>200\)B baseline | 300 median | 0.31 Wh |

citeturn279616search0

Those numbers correspond roughly to output-token intensities ranging from

\[
0.1\text{--}1.4\ {\rm mWh/token},
\]

depending strongly on model size and serving efficiency.

I therefore recommend four deliberately coarse energy classes:

| Class | \(e^{\rm out}\) | Plausible range |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Lite** | **0.00015 Wh/token** | 0.00008–0.00030 |
| **Standard** | **0.00050 Wh/token** | 0.00025–0.00080 |
| **Frontier** | **0.00100 Wh/token** | 0.00050–0.00150 |
| **Frontier+** | **0.00150 Wh/token** | 0.00080–0.00250 |

There are good numerical anchors for these values. The measured Llama-70B results imply around 0.11–0.17 mWh/token; Epoch's GPT-4o estimate gives about 0.6 mWh/token; Oviedo's frontier baseline gives approximately 1 mWh/token. Extremely long DeepSeek measurements reach roughly 1–2 mWh/token. citeturn279616search0turn394271search2

Google's production measurement provides an independent sanity check: its median Gemini Apps prompt consumed **0.24 Wh**, including accelerator, CPU/RAM, idle capacity and data-center overhead. citeturn930895view1

### Model mapping

Because the proprietary companies do not publish enough hardware information to measure each current model independently, the mapping below is explicitly a **model-class assumption**, not a claimed physical measurement.

| Provider | User-visible model family | Class |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | GPT-5.6 Luna | Lite |
| OpenAI | GPT-5.6 Terra | Standard |
| OpenAI | GPT-5.6 Sol | Frontier |
| OpenAI | GPT-5.6 Sol Pro | Frontier+ |
| Anthropic | Claude Haiku | Lite |
| Anthropic | Claude Sonnet | Standard |
| Anthropic | Claude Opus | Frontier |
| Anthropic | Claude Fable | Frontier+ |
| Google | Gemini Flash-Lite | Lite |
| Google | Gemini Flash | Standard |
| Google | Gemini Pro | Frontier |
| xAI | Grok 4.3 | Standard |
| xAI | Grok 4.6 | Frontier |
| DeepSeek | V4 Flash | Standard |
| DeepSeek | V4 Pro | Frontier |

The current product hierarchies themselves are documented by the providers: OpenAI describes Luna, Terra and Sol respectively as its lowest-cost, balanced and flagship GPT-5.6 tiers; Google distinguishes Flash-Lite, Flash and Pro; DeepSeek currently exposes V4 Flash and V4 Pro; and Grok 4.6 is xAI's current frontier model. citeturn910143search8turn980094view1turn357893search5turn910143search2 Anthropic similarly maintains Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and more computationally ambitious Fable-class systems. citeturn357893search1turn357893search7

I would **not** use API price to derive these energy coefficients. Price reflects many commercial factors besides electricity.

---

# 3. Input-token cost

Input and output tokens should not cost the same amount.

During prefill, many input tokens can be processed in parallel; during decoding, output tokens must be generated sequentially. Recent measurements consistently find decoding to dominate normal inference energy. Oviedo et al. therefore approximate effective token length by output tokens for ordinary 500-token inputs, while phase-level measurements find decoding dominant across models. citeturn458839search12turn394271academia43

For very long prompts this approximation eventually breaks down. Epoch AI estimates that a GPT-4o query with 500 output tokens rises from roughly **0.3 Wh** for a short input to about **2.4–2.5 Wh with 10,000 input tokens**, and towards 40 Wh with 100,000 tokens under their transformer-scaling assumptions. citeturn394271search2

I therefore would not use one constant \(e^{\rm in}\). A very simple length-dependent rule is better:

\[
e_m^{\rm in}(L)=
\rho(L)e_m^{\rm out},
\]

with

\[
\boxed{
\rho(L)=
\begin{cases}
0.10, & L\leq1000,\\
0.20, & 1000<L\leq5000,\\
0.35, & L>5000.
\end{cases}}
\]

Thus a Frontier model has

| Visible context | \(e^{\rm in}\) |
|---|---:|
| ≤1,000 tokens | 0.00010 Wh/token |
| 1,001–5,000 | 0.00020 Wh/token |
| >5,000 | 0.00035 Wh/token |

The exact breakpoints are **our interpolation**, rather than provider disclosures. Their purpose is to incorporate two well-supported facts without pretending to reconstruct proprietary serving: short-input prefill is relatively cheap, while long contexts increasingly matter.

This is particularly useful for our application because \(L_i\) is directly reconstructable from the conversation.

---

# 4. Thinking effort

This is necessarily the least directly observable part of text inference.

Modern providers explicitly support different reasoning efforts. ChatGPT currently exposes Medium, High and Extra High for GPT-5.6 Sol; Grok 4.6 exposes low, medium, high and xhigh; DeepSeek V4 exposes adjustable reasoning effort. citeturn910143search0turn910143search10turn357893search6

The web transcript does not contain the true hidden reasoning token count, so we need a prior.

The strongest empirical anchor is again Oviedo et al.:

- ordinary query: median **300 output tokens**, 0.31 Wh;
- test-time-scaling/reasoning query: median **5,000 generated tokens**, 3.91 Wh;
- therefore roughly **16.7× more generated tokens** and **13× more energy**. citeturn279616search0

Epoch's small comparison similarly found o1/o3 producing approximately 1,374–1,392 total tokens versus about 540 for GPT-4o on the same five questions, once hidden reasoning usage was included. citeturn394271search2

I would therefore normalize all provider labels into:

| Thinking level | \(r_\ell\) | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| **None / standard** | **0** | no extra hidden tokens |
| **Low** | **1** | hidden reasoning ≈ visible output |
| **Medium** | **3** | hidden ≈ 3× visible output |
| **High** | **7** | hidden ≈ 7× visible output |
| **Extra-high / Max** | **14** | hidden ≈ 14× visible output |

Thus,

\[
N^{\rm generated}_{\rm effective}
=
(1+r_\ell)N_{\rm output}.
\]

For example, 500 visible tokens under High reasoning are modelled as

\[
500(1+7)=4000
\]

generated computational tokens.

The sequence \(1,2,4,8,15\) for total generation is deliberately simple and spans the empirically observed range from ordinary inference to the approximately 15× longer test-time-scaling regime. **It is a heuristic interpolation**, and the application should say so.

---

# 5. Web search

Here I would use

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm web}=0.04\ {\rm Wh/search}}
\]

for every **visible search query**, in addition to whatever text the LLM subsequently produces.

Google disclosed about 0.3 Wh per conventional search in 2009. Vanderbauwhede updated that figure using changes in PUE and server efficiency, obtaining

\[
0.0003
\frac{1.10}{1.16}
\frac{1}{6.70}
=
0.0000424\ {\rm kWh}
=
0.0424\ {\rm Wh/search}.
\]

citeturn213859search1turn213859search4

This is an extrapolation rather than a new Google measurement, so I would use:

\[
\boxed{0.04\ {\rm Wh}}
\]

with sensitivity

\[
0.02\text{--}0.30\ {\rm Wh/search}.
\]

The tool should count visible search operations only. The LLM's synthesis of search results is already included in token energy and therefore must not be counted again.

---

# 6. Code execution

There is no meaningful universal energy consumption for “running code”: executing `2+2` and training a neural network are obviously different workloads.

For the short calculations ordinarily visible inside conversational assistants, however, serverless measurements give us a useful scale. FaasMeter measured representative server functions at approximately 8–28 J per invocation for operations ranging from simple data movement to image/AES/CNN tasks, corresponding to roughly

\[
0.002\text{--}0.008\ {\rm Wh}.
\]

citeturn355475search64turn355475academia67

I would round upward to

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm code}=0.01\ {\rm Wh/execution}}
\]

with

\[
0.002\text{--}0.05\ {\rm Wh}
\]

as the normal sensitivity interval.

This coefficient is appropriate for **short visible code executions**. A conversation that visibly performs a long simulation, model training or prolonged computation should receive a warning that the estimate probably undercounts that component.

---

# 7. Image input

Luccioni, Jernite and Strubell measured 88 models across ten AI tasks. Their average energy for image captioning—reasonably close to the operation of interpreting an image before answering about it—was

\[
0.063\ {\rm kWh}/1000
=
0.063\ {\rm Wh/image}.
\]

citeturn355475search63turn355475search4

I therefore recommend

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm image,in}=0.06\ {\rm Wh/image}}
\]

with a broad

\[
0.01\text{--}0.20\ {\rm Wh/image}
\]

range.

It is only a proxy because modern multimodal LLMs do not necessarily process images like the captioning models in that benchmark.

---

# 8. Image generation

Here the evidence is much stronger.

In the same FAccT 2024 study, image generation required on average

\[
2.907\ {\rm kWh}/1000
=
2.907\ {\rm Wh/image},
\]

with a standard deviation of 3.31 Wh/image; the reported median was about **1.35 Wh/image**, while the least efficient tested generator reached roughly **11.49 Wh/image**. citeturn355475search63

For an unknown commercial generator, I would use the mean:

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm image,out}=2.9\ {\rm Wh/image}}
\]

and carry a deliberately large range:

\[
\boxed{0.3\text{--}11.5\ {\rm Wh/image}}.
\]

This uncertainty is warranted: image generation differs dramatically with resolution, architecture and denoising steps.

Notice the scale difference. One image can easily represent as much electricity as **thousands of text tokens**.

---

# 9. Video generation

Video is even more variable.

Delavande, Luccioni and Pierrard benchmarked current open text-to-video models on an H100 and measured total GPU+CPU+RAM energy approximately as follows:

| Model | Energy / generated clip |
|---|---:|
| AnimateDiff | 0.14 Wh |
| LTX-Video | 3.79 Wh |
| CogVideoX-2B | 10.08 Wh |
| WAN2.1 1.3B | 22.80 Wh |
| CogVideoX-5B | 25.93 Wh |
| Mochi | 56.06 Wh |
| WAN2.1 14B | 109.47 Wh |

citeturn967734view1turn967734view2

The median of those seven values is approximately **22.8 Wh**. I would round it to

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm video}=25\ {\rm Wh/short\ generated\ clip}}
\]

with

\[
\boxed{0.1\text{--}110\ {\rm Wh}}
\]

as its sensitivity range.

The paper also shows why the range is enormous: energy changes with model size, resolution, frame count and denoising steps. citeturn355475search8

Because an ordinary exported chat frequently does not preserve all those parameters, **25 Wh per generated short clip is about as far as a transcript-only estimator can defensibly go**.

---

# 10. Document analysis

Here I would make a deliberate scientific choice:

\[
\boxed{e_{\rm document}=0}.
\]

This does **not** mean document analysis physically consumes no energy.

It means that I do not think we have sufficient information in a simple web transcript to assign a defensible fixed cost to “one document.” A PDF might contain one page of selectable text or 500 scanned pages requiring OCR, retrieval and repeated model calls; a single constant would therefore be largely meaningless.

The tool should instead say:

> Document processing detected. Additional document-ingestion energy is not separately quantified.

Any text from the document that becomes visible context is already incorporated into token accounting.

This is preferable to introducing an unsupported number simply to make the formula look complete.

---

# 11. Conversion from electricity to water

This required the largest correction to our previous model.

There are **two water terms**:

\[
W=W_{\rm direct}+W_{\rm electricity}.
\]

### Direct data-center water

Recent hyperscaler figures show surprisingly low direct WUE for many modern sites:

- AWS: **0.15 L/kWh** of IT load in 2024; citeturn342384search14
- Meta: **0.19 L/kWh** in 2024; citeturn265285search49
- Microsoft: **0.27 L/kWh** globally in FY2025. citeturn342384search9

Google's LLM-serving fleet is substantially higher: its AI-serving WUE Category 2 was **1.15 L/kWh**, and this is what produces the measured 0.26 mL direct-water value for a 0.24 Wh median Gemini prompt. citeturn930895view1

Because the true server is unavailable to our tool, I would use a neutral modern-hyperscaler central value of approximately

\[
\boxed{K_{\rm direct}=0.2\ {\rm mL/Wh}},
\]

with a broad range of approximately

\[
0.1\text{--}1.1\ {\rm mL/Wh}.
\]

I would **not give Google a worse default solely because Google publishes more detailed water data than the other providers**; doing so would reward opacity.

### Electricity-related water

This component is actually larger in our generic estimator.

EcoLogits uses electricity-mix-specific water-consumption factors and, when server location is unknown, defaults to the world electricity mix. Its current world default is

\[
\boxed{3.908\ {\rm L/kWh}},
\]

which is numerically

\[
\boxed{3.908\ {\rm mL/Wh}}.
\]

citeturn860833search0turn860833search3

This magnitude is credible when compared with the broader electricity-water literature. NREL estimated approximately **1.8 L/kWh** of freshwater consumption for thermoelectric electricity delivered to the end user, while results depend strongly on generation technology and especially on hydropower accounting. citeturn439295search47turn439295search5

For our location-independent tool I therefore propose

\[
\boxed{K_{\rm electricity}=3.9\ {\rm mL/Wh}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
K_W=K_{\rm direct}+K_{\rm electricity}
\simeq0.2+3.9
=4.1\ {\rm mL/Wh}.
}
\]

I would use a sensitivity interval around roughly

\[
\boxed{2\text{--}8\ {\rm mL/Wh}},
\]

because the electricity mix and cooling system can easily dominate the uncertainty.

---

# 12. Frozen parameter table

This is therefore the table I would actually put into the implementation:

| Parameter | Central value | Suggested range | Evidence quality |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Lite output | 0.00015 Wh/token | 0.00008–0.00030 | Good |
| Standard output | 0.00050 Wh/token | 0.00025–0.00080 | Moderate–good |
| Frontier output | 0.00100 Wh/token | 0.00050–0.00150 | Good |
| Frontier+ output | 0.00150 Wh/token | 0.00080–0.00250 | Moderate |
| Input, ≤1k context | \(0.10e_{\rm out}\) | — | Moderate |
| Input, 1k–5k | \(0.20e_{\rm out}\) | — | Moderate |
| Input, >5k | \(0.35e_{\rm out}\) | — | Low–moderate |
| Thinking none | \(r=0\) | — | High |
| Thinking low | \(r=1\) | ~0.3–2 | Low |
| Thinking medium | \(r=3\) | ~1–5 | Low |
| Thinking high | \(r=7\) | ~3–12 | Low |
| Thinking xhigh/max | \(r=14\) | ~7–25 | Moderate upper anchor |
| Web search | 0.04 Wh/search | 0.02–0.30 | Moderate |
| Short code execution | 0.01 Wh/run | 0.002–0.05 | Moderate |
| Image understanding | 0.06 Wh/image | 0.01–0.20 | Moderate |
| Image generation | 2.9 Wh/image | 0.3–11.5 | Good |
| Video generation | 25 Wh/clip | 0.1–110 | Good but highly variable |
| Document surcharge | **0** | unquantified | Deliberate exclusion |
| Direct water | 0.2 mL/Wh | 0.1–1.1 | Moderate |
| Electricity water | 3.9 mL/Wh | ~1.8–8+ | Moderate |
| **Total \(K_W\)** | **4.1 mL/Wh** | **2–8** | Moderate |

## The final estimator

We can now write the complete v1 model compactly as

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
E_{\rm chat} = \sum_i \Big[
& e^{\rm in}_{m_i}(N_i^{\rm in})N_i^{\rm in}\\
&+e^{\rm out}_{m_i}(1+r_\ell)N_i^{\rm out}\\
&+0.04n_i^{\rm web}
+0.01n_i^{\rm code}\\
&+0.06n_i^{\rm img,in}
+2.9n_i^{\rm img,out}\\
&+25n_i^{\rm video}
\Big],
\end{aligned}
}
\]

followed by

\[
\boxed{
W_{\rm chat}^{\rm direct}=0.2E_{\rm chat},
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
W_{\rm chat}^{\rm electricity}=3.9E_{\rm chat},
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
W_{\rm chat}^{\rm total}=4.1E_{\rm chat}\quad{\rm mL}.
}
\]

I think this is now at the right level for the course report: every quantity comes either from the imported chat, from the user's two selections, or from a **small and explicitly documented set of literature-based constants**. The weakest component is hidden reasoning, while image/video generation and the overall energy-to-water conversion have much clearer empirical anchors. Most importantly, we have removed system prompts, cache assumptions, server locations and other variables that an ordinary user cannot observe.

\section{Discussion and outlook}

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence has added a new and increasingly important source of demand to an infrastructure that was already expanding to support the broader digital economy.  Data centres continue to perform predominantly conventional functions, including cloud computing, data storage, web services, content delivery and enterprise applications, and in 2025 these activities were estimated to represent approximately 77\% of global data-centre workloads, compared with 14\% for AI training and 9\% for AI inference~\cite{jll2026outlook}.  The distinction is useful because the environmental footprint of data centres cannot simply be attributed to artificial intelligence; at the same time, the present distribution appears unlikely to remain stable, since AI workloads are projected to approach 50\% of the total by 2030, mainly through the rapid expansion of inference, while almost 100 GW of additional data-centre capacity could be installed over the same period~\cite{jll2026outlook}.  The water footprint examined throughout this report must therefore be understood in the context of a technological system undergoing exceptionally rapid growth, in which improvements in efficiency will develop alongside an increase in the absolute amount of computation demanded by users.

Our analysis has followed this growth from the physical origin of water consumption to the possibilities for reducing it.  Water enters the AI life cycle through semiconductor manufacturing and the construction of computing infrastructure, while during operation it is consumed directly by cooling systems and indirectly through electricity production; the magnitude of these contributions depends strongly on technology and location, which explains the considerable variation among estimates currently found in the literature.  The mitigation strategies discussed in the previous section show that none of these quantities is immutable: improvements in model and hardware efficiency, alternative cooling technologies, reclaimed water, geographical scheduling and intelligent management of computing facilities can all reduce the amount or the environmental relevance of the water required for a given computational service.  These developments are particularly encouraging because AI can itself contribute to this optimisation, extending its role beyond that of a growing consumer of resources to that of a tool for improving the efficiency of data centres, energy systems and other technological infrastructures.

The simple estimator developed in this work approaches the same problem from the opposite end of the system, concentrating on the individual user rather than the operator of the infrastructure.  Its purpose is primarily illustrative: by transforming an ordinary conversation with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok or DeepSeek into an approximate water footprint, it makes a resource demand that is normally invisible during everyday use more tangible and allows the user to observe how longer conversations, greater reasoning effort and computationally intensive tools can affect the resulting estimate.  Such awareness cannot substitute for improvements in infrastructure, but it forms part of the broader sustainability problem because the aggregate demand for AI services ultimately emerges from individual use, and because the rapid expansion of the market provides the economic incentive for corresponding expansion of computing capacity.

More sophisticated approaches already provide considerably more detailed environmental estimates than our deliberately accessible experiment.  EcoLogits, for example, reconstructs the infrastructure required to serve an LLM, estimates GPU and server energy consumption, includes data-centre PUE and WUE, accounts for geographical electricity mixes and can also consider embodied impacts associated with hardware production~\cite{ecologits2025}.  Jegham \emph{et al.} developed an infrastructure-aware framework covering 30 contemporary language models, combining public performance measurements with inferred hardware configurations and regional environmental factors to compare their energy, carbon and water footprints~\cite{jegham2025hungry}.  At the other end of the spectrum, measurements performed directly by Google on its production infrastructure demonstrate the much greater precision that becomes possible when the operator has access to the complete computing stack, including accelerators, host processors, memory, idle capacity and facility overhead~\cite{elsworth2025gemini}.  These approaches make clear that the principal limitation of a user-level estimator is not the absence of increasingly sophisticated methods, but the absence of many of the physical quantities to which those methods should ideally be applied.

This limitation extends beyond the tool proposed here.  EcoLogits explicitly identifies the lack of public information on proprietary model architecture, exact hardware configuration, deployment location, cooling infrastructure and other operational characteristics as a central source of uncertainty in its estimates~\cite{ecologits2025}, while infrastructure-aware studies are often forced to infer these quantities statistically rather than observe them directly~\cite{jegham2025hungry}.  Large AI and cloud providers inevitably measure many aspects of their infrastructure with considerable precision because electricity, cooling, hardware utilisation and capacity determine operating costs, reliability and future investment decisions; nevertheless, the information made available publicly is usually aggregated at the level of a company, fleet or data-centre portfolio, which rarely permits the environmental footprint of a particular model or service to be reconstructed.
